bp: A research code repository is often the place where the practical part of a paper becomes real. The README may name the dataset, describe the source code, mention required tools, point to files, and explain how the artifact should be used. Search systems, artifact indexes, and metadata catalogs need that information in a structured form, not only as paragraphs written for humans. NERdME serves that need by creating a named entity recognition dataset for README files. Named entity recognition means finding spans of text that name important things and assigning each span a type. The paper starts from a gap: scholarly information extraction datasets usually read scientific papers, while implementation details live in code repositories. By manually annotating 200 READMEs with more than ten thousand labeled spans across 10 entity types, the work gives future systems examples of what implementation-level research artifacts look like in the wild.
wh: The hard part is that README files are useful precisely because they are loose. Markdown gives authors headings, lists, links, code blocks, badges, and prose, but it does not force a stable database shape. One repository may introduce a dataset in a sentence, another in a table, another in an install command, and another through a file path or link. Paper-focused extraction data does not solve this, because a scientific paper usually names methods, tasks, citations, and formal claims, while a README names practical objects such as datasets, source code, and other implementation artifacts. The same surface word can play different roles depending on whether it appears in a citation, a command, a heading, or a usage note. A system must therefore decide both where the meaningful span begins and ends and what kind of research artifact that span represents, even when the surrounding Markdown supplies little semantic structure.
naive: A smart beginner might try to reuse an entity extractor trained on scientific papers, then add a few rules for README conventions. For example, headings could be treated as project names, links as artifacts, and capitalized phrases as dataset or software names. That fails because READMEs are not just shorter papers. They mix natural language with file names, commands, dependency lists, dataset references, and project-specific shorthand. A link may be documentation, data, source code, or a citation. A heading may be a usage section rather than an entity. Rules also break when authors use different Markdown styles. The paper's baseline results support this concern: paper-level and implementation-level entities differ clearly enough that README-specific entity types are worth measuring separately.
ap: The core move is to make the missing supervision visible. Instead of assuming that paper-trained data already covers repository artifacts, NERdME builds a small but focused reference set from the setting where the information actually appears: README files. Human annotators mark spans in 200 READMEs and assign them to 10 entity types. Those labels turn free-form repository text into examples a machine can learn from and a test bed researchers can compare against. The paper then uses baseline systems, including large language models and fine-tuned transformer models, to see how existing language tools behave on this new target. It also runs an entity-linking experiment, which asks whether the extracted names can be connected to outside metadata. That downstream step matters because the goal is not merely to color words in READMEs. The goal is to help people discover research artifacts and integrate implementation metadata with scholarly records.
mech: The mechanism begins with a collection of README files from code repositories. Each file enters as Markdown: headings, prose, lists, links, and snippets with no fixed database fields saying, for example, this phrase is a dataset and that phrase is source code. Human annotation then creates the first transformation. Annotators scan the text, choose the exact span boundaries for important mentions, and attach one of 10 entity labels. This produces a record of examples: a span, its surrounding context, and its type. From there, baseline systems can be tested in two ways described by the abstract. A large language model can be asked to read the README and identify entity spans. A fine-tuned transformer can be trained on labeled examples so its internal settings are adjusted toward the labels. Both approaches output predicted spans and types, which are compared with the human labels. The comparison shows how well current tools handle README-specific entities and whether they confuse them with paper-level entities. Finally, the entity-linking experiment takes extracted mentions and tries to connect them to known artifacts or metadata records. The output is therefore not only an extraction score. It is evidence about whether README-derived entities can make repositories easier to index, discover, and connect to the broader scholarly information system.
math: The main mathematical idea is learning from examples. A labeled span is a small teaching case: these words, in this surrounding text, count as this kind of entity. After seeing many such cases, a model estimates a rule that is too detailed to write by hand. The rule is not a single checklist; it is a set of many weighted clues about nearby words, Markdown position, punctuation, names, file-like strings, and context. Fine-tuning means changing those weights to reduce mistakes against the human labels. That is an optimization problem, meaning the system defines what counts as wrong, such as missing a span or assigning the wrong type, and repeatedly changes its settings to make that wrongness smaller. There is also a measurement idea: baseline evaluation compares predicted spans with annotated spans, so boundary choices matter. Calling only half of a dataset name correct may not be enough if an index needs the full name. Entity linking adds a similarity and matching problem: once a mention is extracted, the system must decide which known artifact record, if any, it refers to. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Labels compress messy README language into 10 useful types, but that compression can hide distinctions the 10-type scheme did not include.
dots: This paper sits inside information extraction, but its deeper connection is to the conference-wide problem of turning messy web evidence into usable structure. It is a sibling of retrieval work because extracted README entities become handles for finding artifacts, much as search systems need good document identifiers and metadata. It is also close to language-model evaluation papers, because the baselines test whether general language readers understand a specialized setting or only appear fluent. The repo's information concept frames this as measuring which pieces of text reduce uncertainty: in a README, the useful surprise may be a dataset name, source-code mention, or implementation artifact that a paper-centric extractor would not expect. The broader text-mining family shows the same pattern in other domains: policy clauses, logs, medical abstracts, and harmful content all need task-specific structure. NERdME contributes the repository version of that lesson: the unit to extract must match the world where the decision will be made.
ww: It works because the dataset changes the problem from guessing conventions to comparing against a shared reference. Without labeled READMEs, researchers can argue that their extractor looks reasonable, but they cannot reliably see which entity types it misses or whether paper-trained tools are failing in a systematic way. Human labels create a ground truth for this particular environment. The 10 entity types tell the model which distinctions matter for repository indexing, and the span boundaries teach it how those distinctions appear in free-form Markdown. Baselines are useful because they expose the gap between general language ability and repository-specific extraction. A large language model may understand prose but still miss the exact structured metadata needed by an artifact index. A fine-tuned transformer may improve by repeatedly seeing README examples. The downstream entity-linking experiment gives an additional reason to trust the direction: if extracted README entities can be linked to artifacts and metadata, then the labels are capturing useful objects, not just arbitrary text fragments.
po: The payoff is a new resource for indexing research artifacts in code repositories. NERdME gives the community 200 manually annotated README files, more than ten thousand labeled spans, and 10 entity types aimed at implementation-level details. The baselines show that README entities differ from paper-level entities, so the dataset justifies a separate evaluation target rather than another paper-extraction benchmark. The entity-linking experiment also grounds the work in a practical use case: extracted README entities can help artifact discovery and metadata integration, making code, datasets, and implementation details easier to connect with scholarly records.
limits: The abstract supports the value of the dataset, but it does not prove that 200 READMEs cover all repository styles, research areas, programming languages, or artifact naming habits. The 10 entity types must be the right categories for indexing; useful metadata outside that scheme may be missed. Manual labels are only as reliable as the annotation rules and annotator agreement, which the abstract does not detail. Baseline results show differences between paper-level and implementation-level entities, but not full deployment readiness. Entity linking also assumes that suitable outside artifact or metadata records exist and that extracted mentions are specific enough to match them.
